blocks.text: On the first night of the blackout, you think you're the luckiest person alive. You're locked inside a supermarket. Forty thousand cans of food. All yours.
You're wrong about what matters. Food is the one thing you will never run out of. The water goes on day four. The cold comes for you in the first winter. And people? People take their time.
And in year seven, you'll set this store on fire. With your own lighter. On purpose.

It starts on a Friday, and it starts boring. You stock shelves on the night shift at a big grocery store on the edge of the city. Twenty aisles, a pharmacy, a garden center, a loading dock out back. You put cans in rows until two in the morning, and you put in your headphones, and nobody bothers you.

At eleven forty, the sky over the parking lot turns green. Not a little green. The whole sky. Long glowing curtains of green and red, rippling over the roofs like someone is shaking out a blanket made of light.

You go outside and film it on your phone. Everybody does. You post it with three exclamation marks. You've never seen the northern lights before. You're about a thousand miles too far south to ever see them.

That's the first sign something is very wrong. At eleven fifty-two, the lights in the store start to hum. Then the freezers. Then the hum turns into a buzz you can feel in your teeth. The light above aisle nine explodes in a shower of sparks. And then everything goes dark.

Here's what just happened. The sun throws a giant cloud of charged particles at Earth. A solar storm. When it hits, the sky lights up, and the ground itself fills with electric current. Long metal lines, like power lines, act like antennas. They soak it up.

It's happened before. In September 1859, the biggest solar storm ever recorded hit Earth. It's called the Carrington Event. People saw northern lights as far south as the Caribbean. Telegraph operators got electric shocks. Telegraph paper caught fire. Some lines kept working with the batteries unplugged, running on nothing but the sky.
In 1989, a much smaller storm knocked out the power grid of Quebec in ninety seconds. Six million people in the dark. That one lasted nine hours.

This one is different. Inside every big power station sits a transformer the size of a house. It weighs as much as two hundred cars. And tonight, hundreds of them across the continent overheat and burn out at once. You can't buy a new one at the store. Each one is built by hand, to order, and it takes years.
That part, the part where it takes ten years to fix, is the what if. Everything else in this story, we've tried to keep real.

You walk to the front doors. They're electric. They don't open. The emergency exit is chained from the outside, because the manager is scared of shoplifters. Your phone has no signal. Your manager left at ten. You are alone, locked in, in the dark.
So you do the only thing that makes sense. You grab a headlamp from the camping aisle, you put in fresh batteries, you strap it to your hat, and you go shopping. For free.

Day two. In daylight, the parking lot looks normal. Except nothing moves. Cars sit dead at the traffic lights. A plane is not crossing the sky, because there are no planes. Every car with a computer in it is just a very heavy box now.

You find the stockroom key on the manager's desk, and you do the math. About forty thousand cans. Two thousand gallons of bottled water. Rice, beans, oats, pasta, peanut butter. For one person, that's not a year of food. That's a lifetime.

Canned food lasts much longer than the date on the label. In 1974, scientists opened cans from a steamboat that sank in 1865. The food inside was over a hundred years old. It had lost some vitamins, but it was still safe to eat.

So for three days, it's honestly the best vacation of your life. You eat ice cream for breakfast before it melts. You sleep on a different mattress every night. You ride a shopping cart down aisle twelve at full speed.
On day four, you turn on the tap in the break room. It coughs. It spits air at you. And then nothing.

Here's the part nobody thinks about. City water doesn't flow by itself. Giant electric pumps push it up into water towers, and gravity brings it down to your tap. The water plant had backup generators. Backup generators run on diesel. And the diesel is gone.

That's fine, you tell yourself. You have two thousand gallons of bottled water. And then you count again, the way you should have counted the first time. Drinking, cooking, washing. A person uses about two gallons a day just to stay alive and clean. Two thousand gallons. Three years. If nothing goes wrong.
That night, someone knocks on the loading dock door. Three slow knocks. You stand on the other side, holding a can of beans like a weapon.

I know you're in there. I saw your headlamp. My name is Marta. I live across the street. I ran the pumps at the water plant for thirty-one years. And you're going to waste every drop in that store unless somebody shows you how.
You don't open the door. Not that night. But you think about it until morning.
So stop here for a second. You're alone, with food for a lifetime. A stranger knocks and says she can help. Do you open the door? Write it in the comments. Then see what you did.
On day five, you open it. Marta is sixty-seven. She has a cane, a notebook, and a bucket. She walks past you, straight to the garden center, and starts pulling down rain gutters and plastic barrels.

You're standing on a water tank, she says. Your roof. Look at it. It's flat, it's enormous, and it's covered in drains. This roof is about two acres. One inch of rain on it gives you about fifty thousand gallons.

For two days, you build what Marta calls the ugliest water system in the state. Gutters from the garden center. Hoses. Every plastic barrel the store sells. Rain runs off the roof, through a mesh, into the barrels lined up along the loading dock.

Then she shows you the trick that keeps you alive for ten years. Rainwater isn't clean. It picks up dirt and bird droppings on the roof. So you pour it into clear plastic bottles and leave them in full sun for six hours. The ultraviolet light kills most of the germs. It's real. It's called solar disinfection, and millions of people around the world drink water this way every day.
Boil it if you've got fuel, she says. Sun it if you don't. And never, ever drink from the river. The river is downstream of everybody.

In the second week, a line of cars comes down the road. Old pickups, a school bus, tractors. Anything old enough to run without a computer. Someone with a megaphone is shouting. Camp at the river. Food, doctors, shelter. Last trucks leave at sunset.
You stand at the glass doors and watch them. Then you look back at forty thousand cans. Then at Marta, who can't walk two miles to the river with her cane.
You stay. It's the smartest decision of your life. It will take you seven years to understand why it was also the worst one.

By the end of the first month, the store smells. Not the cans. The freezers. Thousands of pounds of meat and ice cream, all rotting at once. You wrap the whole freezer section in plastic sheets and duct tape, and you never go back there.

Marta makes you write rules on the whiteboard in the break room. Rule one. Never open the front doors. Rule two. No light near the windows after dark. Rule three. Count the food every Sunday. And rule four, the one she underlines twice. Never fire anything indoors. Not a grill, not a generator, nothing.

Here's why. Burning fuel makes carbon monoxide. You can't see it. You can't smell it. It just makes you tired. And then you don't wake up. After big storms and blackouts, it's one of the most common ways people die. Usually from a generator running in a garage.

And the cold comes. The first winter is the hardest thing you've ever done. A supermarket is the worst building in the world to heat. It's a giant metal box with a glass wall. Inside, it's colder than a refrigerator.

So Marta has an idea. The walk-in cooler in the back. Thick walls, foam insulation, one heavy door. For years, it kept the cold in. Now, it keeps the cold out. You drag two mattresses inside, a pile of blankets, and every candle from the seasonal aisle.

A resting person gives off about as much heat as an old hundred-watt light bulb. Two people in a small, insulated room are two light bulbs that never go out. You crack the door for air every hour. Marta sets an alarm on a wind-up kitchen timer. And for the first time in weeks, you sleep warm.

And then you find the best thing in the whole store. Solar garden lights. A whole shelf of them. You stick them on the roof in the daytime, and at night, you bring them in. Every night, forty little suns in a walk-in cooler.
By the end of year one, your gums start bleeding when you brush your teeth. A cut on your hand won't close.

It's scurvy. The disease of old sailors. Your body can't make vitamin C, and there's very little of it left in old cans and dry food. After a few months without it, your body starts falling apart, slowly, from the inside.

Marta's answer is in the garden center and the bulk bins. Dried lentils and mung beans. You soak them in water in jars by the window. Three days later, they sprout. Sprouts are alive, and living sprouts make vitamin C. A handful a day, and your gums stop bleeding in two weeks.

In spring, you build a garden on the roof. Potting soil, seed packets, plastic kiddie pools from the summer aisle. Tomatoes, beans, potatoes, squash. That summer, you eat a tomato you grew yourself, and it's the best thing you've ever eaten.
One night in the fall, you see a light across the parking lot. In the hardware store on the other side. A flashlight, blinking. Short, short, short. Long, long, long. Short, short, short.
SOS. Marta grabs your arm. The headlamp. You flash back with your headlamp. On, off. On, off. Someone over there is alive.

The parking lot is five hundred feet across. You can't shout that far. So Marta takes a kite from the toy aisle and ties it to a spool of fishing line. You wait for the wind to blow the right way. The first kite crashes in a puddle. The ninth one drifts all the way over and drops onto the hardware store roof. A hand grabs it.

By the end of the week, there's a rope across the parking lot. And on the rope, hanging from pulleys, is a shopping cart basket. It goes back and forth all day. On the other side are a teacher named Leo and his two kids. They have tools, a wood stove, and a chainsaw. You have food. It's a very good trade.

In year two, the trucks come. Four old diesel trucks, and men in reflective vests. A diesel engine can run on cooking oil, and they've been draining every fryer in the city. You can smell them coming. They smell like french fries. People call them the Collectors. They collect.

The man in front is calm and polite. His name is Royce. He looks at the store, and the roof garden, and the rope. Nice setup. A lot of glass. It'd be a shame if someone came through that glass at night.

His deal is simple. One fifth of your food every month. And his trucks keep everyone else away. He could try to take the whole store, but people defending a building can hurt a lot of his men. And a store he empties once, he can only rob once.

Before he leaves, he waves you closer. Away from Marta. There's a seat on my truck. Tonight. Clean water, a doctor, a real bed. Just you. All you have to do is open the pharmacy for me. Antibiotics, insulin, painkillers. Out here, a pill is worth more than a gun.

So what do you do? You could take the seat and leave Marta and Leo's kids behind. You could say no and see what Royce does next. Or you could do something nobody has thought of. Write your plan in the comments. Then see what you did.

You tell him the pharmacy is empty. You tell him looters cleaned it out on day two. Royce smiles like you told him a joke. He knows you're lying. And on his way out, his men cut the rope across the parking lot.
Now's a good time to subscribe. Because Royce isn't done with this store. And next time, he won't ask.
Years three and four go by in rhythm. Rain. Sun bottles. Sprouts. The garden. Count the food every Sunday. Every month, you leave one fifth of it on the loading dock, and it's gone by morning.

The world outside gets quieter. Gasoline goes bad in less than a year, so the last regular cars stop. Only the Collectors' trucks still run. People walk. People bike. Some people start walking toward the river, and they don't come back.
The headlamp is your clock now. You've used up eleven packs of batteries. You've got three left. When the last one dies, there will be no light in this store that doesn't come from the sun.

In the winter of year five, Marta doesn't get up to check the barrels. You find her in the cooler, under three blankets, with her notebook open on her chest. It's not Royce. It's not the cold. It's seventy-two years, and five winters without a doctor.
You bury her on the roof, in the garden, under the tomato bed, because the ground outside is frozen solid. Her notebook is full of numbers. Rainfall. Water barrels. Food counts. Days.
On the last page, there's one line, written for you. Leave before the store decides for you.

In year seven, Royce comes back. Not four trucks. Eleven. They park in a circle around the store, with their headlights pointed at the glass. They don't knock. They start cutting through the chains on the front doors.
You have maybe ten minutes. Leo and the kids are with you now, because the hardware store roof caved in last winter. Four people. One back door. And eleven trucks outside.

Then you remember the garden center. Bags of charcoal. Lighter fluid. A whole pallet of it, sitting there for seven summers. And rule four, written on the whiteboard in Marta's handwriting. Never fire anything indoors.
You break the rule. You pour the lighter fluid in a line across the front of the store, between the glass doors and everything you love. And you take out your lighter. On purpose.
The fire goes up like a wall. Black smoke fills the front of the store in seconds. Royce's men stumble back out of the doors, coughing, and nobody can see anything.

You go out the back. Through the loading dock, down the alley, across the creek. No light. Your headlamp stays off. In your backpack, there's water in sun bottles, Marta's notebook, and three packs of seeds.
Behind you, the whole sky turns orange. The store burns all night. Forty thousand cans of food. Seven years of your life.
At sunrise, you reach the river. And you stop. Because there are lights. Real electric lights. In the windows of a camp of wooden houses along the water.

There's an old mill on the river, with a dam and a water wheel. Engineers from the camp rewired it into a small hydroelectric generator. It's not connected to the grid. The sun can't touch it. It just spins, day and night, as long as the river flows.

A woman with a clipboard asks your name. She looks at your notebook, and your sun bottles, and your seeds. How long have you been out there? Seven years. In the supermarket on Route 9? She goes quiet. We've had lights since the second winter. We sent people to tell everyone. The Collectors stopped them on the road. They told everyone in the city the camp had been wiped out.
You spent five years in the dark, a two-hour walk from light. Because one man wanted you to stay where he could find you.

But the camp has problems of its own. The well water makes kids sick. The gardens fail in the shade of the trees. And you know things nobody here knows. How to clean water with nothing but plastic bottles and the sun. How to grow vitamins in a jar. How to keep two people warm in a box.
Within a year, people call you the water guy. You teach classes every Sunday. Leo's kids teach with you. And you count the food every Sunday, out of habit, even though you don't need to.
In year ten, on a cold night in March, a light comes on across the river. Then another. Then a whole street. The new transformers finally made it. The city is coming back, one block at a time.
You stand on the riverbank and watch it, and you switch on your headlamp. It's the last pack of batteries. You've been saving it for ten years. You just didn't know what for.

You called staying in that store the biggest mistake of your life. But if you'd gotten on that truck in week two, Marta would have died alone in her apartment. Leo's kids would have starved behind a door you never knocked on. And nobody at the river would know how to clean a glass of water.
So, was it a mistake? Tell me in the comments.
